speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: asked the Minister for Law (a) whether an update can be provided on the cases undertaken by the Public Defender’s Office (PDO) since it commenced operations on 1 December 2022; and (b) how does the PDO deal with cases involving alleged crimes that may be viewed by the public as being morally repugnant in assessing whether to provide legal aid.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Public Defender’s Office (PDO) was set up in December of 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we are now about 12 months into it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is to provide criminal defence aid to persons facing non-capital charges and who cannot afford a lawyer.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With this co-delivery model, CLAS’ annual case load in 2023 is expected to be lower than in 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Nonetheless, this has only been nine to 10 months, and we have to continue to monitor the situation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of the applicants for criminal defence aid face charges for minor offences, like shop theft, mischief and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The means test, in terms of economic means; and the merits test, in terms of having some basis for defence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The means test, as I said earlier, is to ensure that aid is given to those who are unable to afford legal fees.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The merits test assesses whether the applicant will benefit from legal representation or has reasonable grounds to defend or appeal his case in Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sometimes, the PDO comes across cases, which many would consider to be highly represensible.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It can relate to sexual assault, child abuse or family violence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The nature of the crime can cause public outrage or concern.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the PDO cannot refuse to handle these cases.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The test is not one of moral reprehensibility.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has to handle the cases, as long as they are assessed to have some legal merit.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One example is a recent Court of Appeal matter involving an accused person who pleaded guilty to sexually penetrating his own younger sister.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think almost all right-thinking members of society would say that it is completely unacceptable, reprehensible.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He had committed the offences when he was between the age of 15 and 17 years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was initially sentenced to 18 years in prison and 16 strokes of the cane.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He applied to PDO for aid to appeal against his sentence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This scenario sometimes arises in other jurisdictions as well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You have the case of Police Constable Andrew Harper in the United Kingdom.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A uniformed officer gave chase to a group of teenagers who were trying to escape after stealing a bike.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was dragged by the car which was driven by one of the teenagers and he died.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There was widespread public sympathy for him and outrage over the fact that he died.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court found them guilty of manslaughter instead of murder.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In another case in New Zealand, a family of five was mass murdered, and David Bain, who was the only survivor, was accused of the murder.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This case has been described as, and I quote, "the most widely discussed and divisive in New Zealand's criminal history".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After 13 years, he was acquitted of all charges.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Without legal aid, he might have remained behind bars until today.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I explained in my Ministerial Statement in April last year, the provision of legal aid cannot depend on public outrage against the alleged offender or sympathy for the victim.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With the PDO, we will assess each case based on its own merit, and those who have a meritorious case but cannot afford a lawyer will be provided access to legal advice and representation to defend their case in court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is how we can try to ensure that access to justice is available to more.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is actually in line with the ethos of lawyers in the Criminal Bar.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recall the words of the late Mr Subhas Anandan, known as one of the doyens in the Criminal Bar, and he said that everybody deserves a fair trial, including those who have been accused of committing heinous crimes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Sometimes, PDO officers may deal with requests on the part of such accused person to put certain lines of questions to vulnerable victims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And PDO officers, based on their assessment, they may not want to take up such lines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, cross-examining a vulnerable victim in relation to the person's sexual background and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How do we protect PDO officers in these circumstances?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Because what we do not want also, is to have an allegation made against such a PDO officer and he has to deal with it in the disciplinary setting.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would say the framework of the law is clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What you can ask, what you cannot ask in cross-examination, lawyers will know.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The PDO is led by a very senior lawyer who will give guidance to the more junior lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And ultimately in Court, there is the prosecution and there is the Court, which controls proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the line to be crossed in terms of misconduct, is quite far; there are a number of safeguards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not believe that our PDO officers feel that they have to pull back from proper questioning, or be particularly concerned that questions they ask will be considered beyond the pale, in terms of correct and proper discharge of a lawyer's duties in court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, in any event, I will pass on the Member's feedback to the Chief Public Defender.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That is the point I was trying to raise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the answer to that is: it is a situation faced by all lawyers who practise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you think is the right defence or the right case to put forward?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are assessments and it depends on training and skill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By and large, the Legal Service gets very good officers who apply to join.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: PDO gets very committed officers and it depends on training.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the whole approach for PDO officers and AGC officers, the prosecution: you do your duty without fear or favour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We look forward to receiving more detailed data about the actual effect on it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note earlier that the Minister said that the amount that CLAS handles this year is expected to be lower, because of the coming on stream of the PDO.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to the means and merit test, I think we are in broad alignment of the principles used to decide whether or not the PDO will take on the cases.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the capacity, it is chicken and egg.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mean, it depends on how many cases come up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At present, there is a certain pathway where PDO is intended to build up from last year, based on our assessment of the number of cases that are likely to come up, bearing in mind that we really do not want to go in to territory where lawyers are providing services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want to meet the demand, where the clients today, either by themselves or through their family, are unable to pay for lawyers to represent them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because this is taxpayers' money and it has got to be used judiciously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have made that point before several times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are a number of countries which have gone down this route and then find that they are unable to afford it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If people can afford it, they should go and pay for it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Precisely how many cases we will take up, it is subject to how many cases apply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a balance between the well-known manpower shortage all across Singapore, including in the legal industry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fact is that, as a result of our new approach taken a few years ago to drugs, where we no longer prosecute a drug abuser as a criminal, but send such a person to rehabilitation, that has removed a lot of cases from the criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because these people are now in rehabilitation and then, they are released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even if they come back for the third time or a fourth time, as long as they only abuse drugs and they have not committed any other offence, they are no longer charged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the number of criminal cases have come down quite substantially.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Crimes like these have been redefined as we take a rehabilitation approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With all that, we will look at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the number of cases go up, we will employ more people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or if we cannot, we will explain that this is our capacity and this is what we are prepared to spend.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, it is up to Parliament to say, "We think you ought to spend more of taxpayers' money." We will come and discuss that, as necessary.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I was not suggesting that it was because of capacity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Given that this is a new office, I am just curious about whether we have had overcapacity?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: And what are the anticipated cases, what we budgeted for and also what eventually came to pass over the last 11 to 12 months?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The second point was about the two means and merits testing, the two broad categories that the Minister mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I just wanted to know, as a separate issue, how many cases were actually rejected because of it?
